# Two exact obstructions to stronger arithmetic-tail shortcuts

The target still under investigation is

`S_d(q+1)^(1/(d+1))+S_d(q-1)^(1/(d+1))
 <=2 S_d(q)^(1/(d+1))`, `d>=1`, `q>1`,

where `S_d(q)=sum_(j>=0)(q-j)_+^d`. Nothing in this note refutes that
target. It certifies two stronger assertions that cannot be used to
prove it.

## 1. Unit-shift monotonicity of the continuous derivative is false

Let `F(q)=S_2(q)^(1/3)`. At the positive integers, `S_2` is
differentiable and `S_2'(q)=2 S_1(q)`, because a newly appearing term
has value and first derivative zero. Hence

`F'(2)=2/5^(2/3)`, `F'(3)=4/14^(2/3)`.

Both are positive and

`F'(3)^3-F'(2)^3=64/196-8/25=8/1225>0`.

Thus `F'(q+1)<=F'(q)` is false. It is insufficient to replace the
desired unit-interval integral comparison by a pointwise derivative
comparison. The actual midpoint inequality for `d=2` is proved in
`candidate 5dfdef886fd3ea86`.

## 2. Poisson-binomial mixtures of binomial coefficients can be convex

Consider the candidate statement that for every Poisson-binomial random
variable `V` with at most `k-1` Bernoulli trials, the integer sequence

`m -> [E binom(m+k-V,k)]^(1/k)`

is concave at `m>=1`, with the binomial coefficient interpreted as zero
when its integer top is less than `k`.

This is false with `k=3` and `V~Binomial(2,1/2)`. In this case

`F_m=E binom(m+3-V,3)
 =(1/4)binom(m+3,3)+(1/2)binom(m+2,3)
   +(1/4)binom(m+1,3)
 =[(m+1)^3+(m+1)/2]/6`                                (1)

for every integer `m>=0`. The polynomial binomial formulas in (1) agree
with the stated truncation even at `m=0`, where the two lower terms
have integer tops `2` and `1` and vanish.

Set `x=m+1`, `P(x)=x^3+x/2`. For a positive function `P`, the second
derivative of `P^(1/3)` has the sign of

`P P''-(2/3)(P')^2`.

Here the expression is exactly

`x^2-1/6>0` for `x>=1`.

Thus the real extension of `F_m^(1/3)` is strictly convex throughout
`m>=0`. The desired concavity fails at every integer midpoint `m>=1`;
discarding the first endpoint does not repair the assertion.

The first three exact values are `F_0=1/4`, `F_1=3/2`, `F_2=19/4`.
An independent radical certificate of the first violation is

`1+19^(1/3)>11/3>2*6^(1/3)`.

The first strict comparison follows from `19>(8/3)^3`; the second
follows from `(11/3)^3>48`. Multiplying by `4^(-1/3)` gives the strict
reverse of midpoint concavity for these three values.

The generating function of this sequence is
`(1+t)^2/[4(1-t)^4]`. Its numerator has only negative real roots and
its coefficients are a Poisson-binomial probability law. Consequently
these properties alone do not prove the desired arithmetic-tail
inequality. An argument using the particular Euler--Frobenius
numerators of the actual power sums must retain additional structure.
